scenario.title: Technika, hibaelhárítás
scenario.persona: An intermediate cook whose last schnitzel came out greasy with the breading falling off. A bit frustrated, wants to understand why.
scenario.goal: Understand what went wrong and how to get crispy schnitzel with breading that sticks, using the collection's Chicken Schnitzel recipe.
successCriteria: The assistant refers to the Chicken Schnitzel recipe from the collection
It names concrete causes (e.g. oil temperature, drying the chicken, the breading order) and the oil temperature from the recipe

messages.content: Hey, I tried making Chicken Schnitzel recently, but it came out greasy and the breading was falling off. I was following the recipe in the collection, but something clearly went wrong. Can you help me figure out what might have caused this and how to get a crispy schnitzel with the breading sticking well? Also, what oil temperature should I be aiming for according to the recipe?

Greasy and the breading slipping off usually come down to moisture and oil temperature/handling. Looking at the Chicken Schnitzel recipe in the collection, here’s how to dial it in and what likely went wrong.

Oil temperature in the recipe
- Step 6: Heat oil to 375°F.

Why it got greasy (and how to fix it)
- Oil too cool: If you started below 375°F or crowded the pan, the temp dropped and the crust soaked oil. Preheat to 375°F and fry in small batches so the oil stays around 350–370°F. Let the oil recover between batches. A cast-iron skillet (as in the recipe) helps keep the heat steady.
- Not enough oil or wrong pan: Too-shallow oil or a thin pan can cause sticking and temp swings. Use enough neutral oil so the cutlets can sizzle freely (shallow-fry depth) and avoid overcrowding.
- Steam and sogginess post-fry: Drain on a wire rack (the recipe’s Step 10), not paper towels, and salt immediately.

Why the breading fell off (and how to fix it)
- Surface moisture: After the 30-minute brine (Step 2), pat the chicken very dry before pounding and dredging (Steps 3–5). Any leftover moisture makes the coating slide.
- Dredging technique: Go flour → egg → panko (Step 7). Dust with a thin, even coat of flour and shake off the excess; globs of flour turn to paste and peel off. Let excess egg drip. Press panko on firmly, including the edges.
- Rest before frying: The recipe has you keep prepped cutlets on a wire rack (Step 8). From general cooking practice, letting them rest on that rack 5–10 minutes helps the crumbs hydrate and stick.
- Moving too soon: Even though the recipe says to turn often (Step 9), give the cutlet 30–45 seconds undisturbed at the start so the crust can set, then turn gently and often. Use a wide fish spatula or tongs with a light touch.
- Overcrowding: Too many pieces make you jostle them and drop the temp—both can knock the coating off.

A couple more small checks
- Pound evenly to about 1/4 inch (Steps 3–4) so they cook fast and crisp before the coating loosens.
- If you used all butter to fry: the recipe notes you can use half butter, half oil; using only butter can scorch and promote sticking. Stick to neutral oil (or half-and-half) at 375°F.

If you want, tell me what pan you used, whether you had a thermometer, and how many cutlets you fried per batch—I can pinpoint exactly where things went sideways and help you nail it next time.
